paras: The lynching of Judson Cason was the killing of a Black man, accused of cutting John L. Bryan, who was seized near Lloyd's Station, Jefferson County, Florida, on election day, November 6, 1888, and found dead in the Miccosukie Sinks. A coroner's jury named eight men, among them Bryan, and a grand jury reportedly indicted four while Bryan remained a fugitive. Northern papers took particular notice because Bryan was the son of the writer Mary E. Bryan, who said her son thought he was doing right.

About a month earlier, Bryan was seriously cut with a knife in a fight in a mill house at Lloyd's Station. Cason, described as "a negro" living just over the line in Leon County, was charged with the cutting, although the Savannah Morning News said there was no positive evidence of who had done it. Judge Puleston issued a warrant for Cason's arrest, and it was placed in the hands of Lee Houston to serve.
Mrs. Bryan later said she had been urged to come to Florida before the election because her son, active in politics, might get into trouble "with the negroes at the polls" at Lloyd's.

On the evening of election day, Houston, Bryan and Arthur Duncan went to Cason's house and drew him away on the pretense that he was needed at Lloyd's Station. Once across the county line he was told he was a prisoner, his hands were tied, and he was delivered at Lloyd's to Gus Simmons, who said he would take him to Monticello in the morning; meanwhile he was held under guard in the depot warehouse.

Early in the night he was put in a wagon and carried two miles to the Miccosukie Sinks, bound hand and foot according to the later Morning News account. His body, "frightfully cut up" and weighted with five or six rocks, was found on Thursday. According to the Morning News, it had lodged on a ledge instead of vanishing into the sinks.

A coroner's jury named John L. Bryan, Alfred Duncan, Lee Houston, Jefferson Thompson, Lee Taylor, Charles S. Russell, Augustus Saunders and W. A. Simmons, whom the World called "suspected parties" and the Tribune said were charged with the murder. Simmons was reported arrested. A Monticello dispatch of November 23 said instead that the jury charged six men, only one was captured, the grand jury indicted Bryan, Houston, Duncan and Gus Simmons, and the others turned state's evidence.
Bryan was reported a fugitive near his home, still suffering from his wound; his mother's lawyer advised him to surrender. No report of a surrender or trial appears in the coverage found.

The first report found ran in the Savannah Morning News's Florida column on November 12; a fuller Monticello dispatch, printed by the Wichita Eagle as "Horrible Punishment of a Colored Man," said the affair had "set the people wild." In New York the Evening World printed a Jacksonville special headed "Sunk Him in Miccosukie Sinks," about "a West Florida negro accused of crime," and the Washington Evening Star reprinted it the same day. The New-York Tribune's Monticello special was headlined "A Negro Entrapped and Murdered" and "an unusually brutal crime even for Florida 'crackers,'" and it closed by noting that a Republican, Jesse D. Cole, had been driven from the county before the election.

Later coverage centered on Bryan's mother: the Morning News headlined its November 24 story "Miccosukie's Red Crime" over "One of the murderers a son of Mrs. Mary E. Bryan," and a Jacksonville wire printed in Kenosha, Wisconsin, led with her son's flight. It also reprinted a Monticello Constitution interview in which Mrs. Bryan said her son had lived in Louisiana and Arkansas, "where six men constitute a court," and thought he was doing "perfectly right."

Accounts of how Cason died differed. The Jacksonville special said he was probably put in the water alive, and the Monticello dispatch and Kenosha wire said he was believed to have died of strangulation. The Morning News's November 23 account said he was stabbed to death at the sinks with at least a dozen wounds. The Wichita Eagle's copy also dated the seizure to Thursday evening rather than Tuesday.

reader.title: Lynching of Judson Cason
bases: A Black man held on a warrant for cutting a white man was taken at night from a guarded warehouse by several men, killed and sunk in a sinkhole (A2, A4, A7).

Cason, arrested on a warrant for cutting Bryan, was carried from custody and killed without legal process; a coroner's jury named eight (or six) men and a grand jury indicted four (A2, A4, A7). Bryan's mother said her son believed Cason had stabbed him and thought, as where 'six men constitute a court,' he was doing right (A7).

The New York World's Jacksonville special, the Tribune's Monticello special and the Savannah Morning News's Monticello reports agree on the seizure, the killing and the sinks, and the later Morning News account adds the indictments and the accused's mother's admission (A2, A4, A7); the early texts share wording and may rest on one local account (A1, A4, A5).

accounts.label: Monticello and Jacksonville reports
accounts.gist: Cason was enticed across the county line, bound, held under guard at Lloyd's, carried to the sinks at night and found cut up and weighted with rocks; a coroner's jury named eight men.

accounts.label: Morning News Monticello follow-up
accounts.gist: Cason was stabbed to death at the sinks with a dozen wounds and thrown in; the jury charged six, the grand jury indicted four, others turned state's evidence.

accounts.label: Accused's mother (Mary E. Bryan)
accounts.gist: Her son believed Cason had stabbed him and, having lived where 'six men constitute a court,' thought he was doing right; he would surrender when well enough.

framing.detail: The Tribune headlined 'A Negro Entrapped and Murdered' and 'an unusually brutal crime even for Florida crackers,' and noted a Republican had been driven from the county.
The World special, reprinted by the Evening Star, ran as 'Sunk Him in Miccosukie Sinks: Shocking Treatment of a West Florida Negro Accused of Crime.'
A Monticello dispatch called it 'the most horrible affair that was ever perpetrated in this county'; the Wichita Eagle headed it 'Horrible Punishment of a Colored Man.'
The Morning News headlined 'Miccosukie's Red Crime' and called the men murderers, but devoted much of the story to Mrs. Bryan's 'pathetic' account and her defense of her son.
